A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LocoVR study. Their main text, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained, revised and added content.

before.justification: v1 reports original dataset statistics, evaluations of three prediction tasks, ablations, GIMO testing and social-navigation case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds scene-map experiments and further analyses of trajectories and participants.

M1.justification: Appendix D.2 adds U-Net+A* variants using height or semantic maps instead of binary obstacle maps, a limited input adaptation. The capture system, core architectures, losses and prediction procedures remain unchanged; Appendix F.5 clarifies existing inverse-kinematics processing.

E1.justification: The same LocoVR, GIMO, THOR-MAGNI and LocoReal data and three prediction tasks remain. The added map-input experiment and behavioral analyses use existing LocoVR coverage without establishing new scenes, populations or task requirements.

E2.justification: Comparator membership in Tables 2–10 is unchanged, including Ynet, U-Net, A* variants, RANDOM and NEAREST in their respective tasks. Appendix D.2 compares input variants of the existing model; newly cited social-navigation methods are not added benchmark competitors.

E3.justification: Appendix H changes the stated global-path window from 7 seconds (1 past, 6 future) to 10 seconds (1 past, 9 future), although Figure 9 still shows 6 future seconds. v2 also adds within-LocoVR map-input evaluation and trajectory summary measures, and revises the participant count from 31 to 32. These changes do not establish that existing benchmarks were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a focused binary/height/semantic-map comparison and analyses of path efficiency, walking speed, speed peaks and closing speed. Existing dataset-scale, second-person and heading-direction ablations, GIMO testing and social-navigation case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Three-trial means and standard deviations remain specified in the main table captions, and GIMO testing retains five random splits. Removing the standalone reproducibility statement does not remove these disclosures. The new map experiment uses the existing three-trial reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 2–10 retain their numerical results. New results include Table 11, mean path efficiency of 0.81, walking speed around 0.8 m/s and participant statistics. Table 11 prints a semantic-map error of 1.70 versus binary-map 0.183 at 3–6 m, contradicting the prose's blanket improvement claim.

T1.justification: No theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations change. The added explanation of the standard path-efficiency ratio supports an empirical descriptive analysis rather than introducing new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion replace full-body-pose or full-body-motion claims with accurate trajectories; Section 3.1 specifies auxiliary sparse tracker data. This narrows the claimed data product while retaining the central contributions of large-scale two-person collection and improved performance across three tasks.

C2.justification: Appendix J shifts from describing VR/real discrepancies toward mitigation through avatars, filtering and real-world evaluation, removing the image-domain-gap discussion. New passages discuss inverse-kinematics limitations, defend two-person applicability, propose mechanisms involving object height and semantics, and broaden potential applications beyond the evaluated tasks.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents sparse tracker outputs and avatar reconstruction limitations, describes filtering trajectories that pass through virtual objects, and supplies participant ages, genders and pair relationships. It also changes the reported dataset/code repository address. Core hardware, hyperparameters, architectures and training-time disclosures remain.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands positioning against social-navigation datasets such as SIT, SACSON and SocNav1 and adds a subsection on VR systems for human-motion analysis. Numerous relevant works are added, while the earlier Mead proxemics references and James domain-adaptation reference are removed.

P1.justification: Rewriting concentrates on related work, limitations and Appendix J, while the main evaluation narrative and implementation descriptions remain largely intact. Appendices D and I gain subsections, front matter is updated, and acknowledgments replace the standalone reproducibility statement.

P2.justification: The appendix displays are substantially revised: four cumulative plots become histograms, four additional behavioral plots and a map-comparison figure appear, and Tables 11–13 are added. Table 1 is compressed and loses its semantics column. Most existing main figures and benchmark tables are retained.

improvement.justification: Clearer trajectory-versus-body-pose claims, participant documentation, behavioral characterization and broader research positioning provide a limited net improvement. The main benchmark evidence remains unchanged. Gains are constrained by Table 11's numerical/interpretive inconsistency, the conflicting future-window descriptions in Appendix H and Figure 9, and the removal of some explicit VR-to-real limitations.
